title: Septic Urgency Assessment
intro: Nine questions about what your system is actually doing. You get a severity reading, what it means, and what to do next — before you call anyone.

results.headline: This needs attention today.
results.meaning: What you have described is an active failure, not a maintenance issue. Sewage in living space is a biohazard, surfacing effluent is a groundwater concern in Middle Tennessee's fractured limestone, and a sounding alarm means the system is telling you it cannot cope.
steps: Stop all water use now — no flushing, laundry, dishwasher or showers. Every gallon makes it worse.
Keep people and pets away from any affected area, indoors or out.
Do not try to plunge or chemically clear it.
Call us. If the backup reached living space, photograph it before any cleanup for your insurer.

results.headline: Get this looked at within days, not months.
results.meaning: Several signs point to a system at or beyond capacity. It has not failed outright yet, which is the useful part — acting now is the difference between a pump-out and a drain field. Symptoms returning soon after a pump-out in particular suggests a failed baffle, a blocked filter or a field problem rather than a full tank.
steps: Reduce water use — spread laundry across the week, fix running toilets.
Book a pump-out with an internal inspection, not just an empty-and-go.
Ask specifically for the baffles and effluent filter to be checked and reported.
Keep vehicles and heavy equipment off the drain field.

results.headline: Early signs. Worth acting on while it is cheap.
results.meaning: Individually these are minor, but together they are the front end of the usual failure sequence. Systems rarely fail suddenly — they signal for months first. Everything you are seeing is addressable now at routine-service prices.
steps: Book a pump-out if it has been three or more years.
Have the effluent filter cleaned and the baffles inspected while the tank is open.
Note whether symptoms track with wet weather — that points at the field rather than the tank.
Get the interval set from measured sludge depth rather than a rule of thumb.

results.headline: Nothing here suggests a problem.
results.meaning: No failure signals from what you have described. The useful thing now is keeping to a genuine interval — Tennessee guidance is every three to five years, and every two to three with a garbage disposal, a larger household or a smaller tank.
steps: Book on schedule rather than on symptoms.
Ask for sludge and scum depth to be measured so your interval reflects your tank.
Have the effluent filter cleaned at each visit.
Consider risers if the lids are buried — they pay back in two or three services.
